statements.wording: Says no more than the AF-1 headline. Limitations in §4A (one garden behind three NZ sources; UC IPM tied to dry climates) and the variety-choice condition in the NZ quotations are not in the text.
statements.note: Matches the AF-1 headline and §6.1. Read alone it leaves out three things the record states: §4A "Three of the New Zealand sources describe one garden; UCIPM-DIS ties its statement to dry climates" (UCIPM-DIS: "especially in California's dry interior valleys"), and that the New Zealand sources tie it to variety choice (NZRS-FAQ: "Yes you can. Grow varieties that are very disease tolerant."; ABG-R: "We only grow those that perform well and stay healthy without spraying."). AF-1 is High, so rule §3 does not require its limits to be stated; item 2 follows it in the same answer.

statements.wording: Follows the headline. "may not last" is quoted in §4 from the RHS only (two pages, one voice).
statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: "with its limits stated"): the §4A limits are not in the text. C-3 is not presented as a disagreement (rule 2); ARC §6.1 does not present it as one either.
statements.note: Matches the AF-3 headline. Two things to know. (1) In §4 the "may not last" half is quoted only from the RHS (RHS-BS: "this usually does not last"; RHS-PM: "may not persist for the lifetime of the plant"), which §8.1 counts as one voice; UMD-BS speaks only to region ("resistance can be regionally variable"), and the ZLESAK quotation ("Race-specific resistance was generally more prevalent in newer rose cultivars") does not itself say resistance fails. (2) AF-3 is Moderate, and its §4A limitation "RHS is one voice; contrasted with Auckland experience (C-3)" is not in the text, so a gardener is not told this is a point on which sources differ (C-3).

statements.wording: "Sources say" for a claim that §4 shows one source making (RHS-BS: "Popular garden cultivars of hybrid teas, floribundas, climbers and patio types are often susceptible."). "to disease" is not in the finding.
statements.rules: Rule 1 (shows how strong the agreement is): one source presented as several.
statements.note: "Sources say" (plural) is not borne out by §4. The only quotation in AF-4 for the susceptibility claim is RHS-BS: "Popular garden cultivars of hybrid teas, floribundas, climbers and patio types are often susceptible." The other three AF-4 sources (ARS-FUNG, UMD-BS, RSNSW) are quoted on needing fungicide, not on which roses are susceptible. The statement also adds "to disease": the finding says only "are susceptible", and the one quotation is from the RHS black spot page. Supported wording: attribute the claim to the RHS as the one source §4 quotes for it, keeping its "often susceptible", and drop "to disease". Note for the ROC: ARC §6.1 words this the same way ("Many popular Hybrid Teas and Floribundas are susceptible (AF-4, Moderate)"), so the builder followed §6.1; the single-source basis shows only in the §4 quotations.

statements.wording: Follows the AF-4 headline and §6.1. ARS-FUNG quotation says "some application", not regular; UMD-BS quotation says "Most people", not susceptible roses. "The view above" depends on position.
statements.rules: Rule 2 met: better-supported view first, and who disagrees is named.
statements.note: Matches AF-4, C-1 and §6.1, and is more careful than §6.1 about the Rose Society of NSW. Four things to know. (1) "The view above" has no meaning if the statement is shown on its own, and even in place it does not say which of items 1 to 5 is "the view". (2) The quotations do not quite say what is attributed: ARS-FUNG says "requires some application of fungicides, especially when conditions support disease development" (not "regular"), and UMD-BS says "Most people will need to use labeled fungicide sprays every 7-14 days" (not "susceptible roses"). The blend "susceptible roses need regular fungicide" is the ARC's own (AF-4 headline, §6.1), not the builder's. (3) "an American Rose Society article" follows §6.1, but §8.1 records ARS-FUNG as "one rosarian's article from a local rose society newsletter, hosted by the American Rose Society" and §4A as "an individual rosarian"; a gardener may read it as the Society's position. (4) The level shown is Moderate (AF-4, correct by the first-trace rule), but it sits on a sentence that also says "The view above is the better supported", and could be read as confidence in that judgement. The RHS side of C-1 is in item 7, not here.

statements.wording: "Sources say" for "most common", which §4 shows one source saying (RSNSW) and §4A flags: "'Most common' is stated by one rose society."
statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated) not met; rule 1 (how strong the agreement is) not met for "most common".
statements.note: "Sources say black spot is the most common fungal disease of roses": §4 shows one source for "most common" (RSNSW: "It is the most commonly occurring fungal disease on roses."), and §4A records it as the finding's limitation: "'Most common' is stated by one rose society." AF-8 is Moderate, which rule §3 allows "with its limits stated"; the limit is in the package's Limitation column but not in the words a gardener sees. The second half ("needs leaves to stay wet") is supported by two sources (UCIPM-BS: "leaves must remain wet for more than about 7 hours"; GU-DIS: "Mild temperatures and wet leaf surfaces encourage black spot infection"). Supported wording: attribute "most common" to the one rose society that says it (the Rose Society of NSW), and keep "sources say" for the wet-leaf half. Note for the ROC: §6.1 words it the same way without the limit.

statements.wording: Follows the headline. Conditions in the quotations (mid-morning or midday; dry weather) are not carried. "the exception" depends on the preceding statement.
statements.note: Matches the AF-18 headline, and carries its limitation (RHS-PM: long-wet leaves "may favour other diseases"). Two things to know. (1) The quotations are narrower than "water on the leaves can reduce it": RHS-PM: "Overhead watering (in mid-morning) in dry weather can reduce powdery mildew"; UCIPM-DIS: midday sprinkling "may limit the disease". The time of day and "in dry weather" are not in the text. (2) "is the exception" refers back to item 5 and has no referent if shown alone.

statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated): the limit is not in the text.
statements.note: Matches the AF-20 headline and keeps its hedge ("describe ... as"). AF-20 is Moderate; its limitation in §4 ("None gives a mechanism or measure.") and §4A ("No mechanism or measure given.") is in the package's Limitation column but not in the gardener-facing words.

statements.wording: ok as a collective statement. Potassium bicarbonate is named by one of the three (UC IPM).
statements.note: Supported as a statement of what the three US extension services name between them (UC IPM, Clemson, Wisconsin). To know: potassium bicarbonate is named only by UC IPM (UCIPM-DIS, UCIPM-BS; one programme per §8.1); Clemson's list is "for powdery mildew" and Wisconsin's is for black spot, so no one source names all three for both diseases. §4A limitation not in the text: "Wisconsin says neem oil gives only 'some' control" (WISC-BS: "has been shown to provide some black spot control"). AF-21 is High, so its limits need not be stated. The builder left out the finding's "lower-toxicity" label; that says less, not more.

statements.wording: Follows §6.1. "in other countries" implies the US position is known; R-1 lists the US among the countries not established.
statements.rules: Rule 5: the gap is said. No pointer to local help; the label reminder (item 8) follows in the same answer.
statements.note: Matches AF-40 and §6.1; "Three US universities" is correct (UCIPM-BS, CLEM-DIS, WISC-BS all name chlorothalonil). To know: "in other countries" follows §4A ("outside the US") and §6.1 ("elsewhere"), but R-1 is wider: "Which spray types are currently approved for home-garden use on roses in New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US", and AF-34 records "No Australian or US regulator page was read". The wording can be read as meaning US approval was established; it was not checked. The finding also has one Australian nursery (ROSS-SP) naming triforine and mancozeb; "These are US sources" is true of the three universities named.

statements.rules: Rule 7 wording met. ARC §7 item 5 only partly met: "use only a product labelled for roses where they live" is not in the reminder.
statements.note: ARC §7 item 5 says: "Wherever a spray is described, tell the gardener to use only a product labelled for roses where they live and to follow its label (rule 7)", and §6.2 R-1 says the same. This reminder gives "follow its label and your local rules" but not "use only a product labelled for roses where they live"; that sentence appears only in PKR-CGD-000014 item 2. The reminder itself matches rule 7 ("follow the label and the local rules").

statements.wording: Follows the headline and §6.1. "They don't cure it" drops UCIPM-DIS's "generally" and the §4A limitation that ARS-FUNG mentions curative products.
statements.note: Matches the AF-7 headline and §6.1 word for word ("They don't cure it"). To know: the flat second sentence is firmer than the quotations. UCIPM-DIS: "generally you must apply them to prevent rather than eradicate infections"; and §4A records the limitation "ARS-FUNG also mentions curative products for established infection." AF-7 is High, so its limits need not be stated.

statements.wording: Follows the headline, but "is needed" is firmer than the quotations ("consider", "may need") and §4A ("Stated conditionally, without a measure").
statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated): the limit is not in the text.
statements.note: Equivalent to the AF-11 headline ("Spraying need and frequency rise with wet weather, a history of disease, or a heavy outbreak"). To know: (1) the quotations are conditional and "is needed" is not: WISC-BS: "consider applying preventative fungicide treatments" where "your rose has a history of severe black spot, and the weather for the growing season is predicted to be wet"; ARS-FUNG: "especially when conditions support disease development"; RSNSW: "they may need to be sprayed more frequently." §4A limitation: "Stated conditionally, without a measure." AF-11 is Moderate and this limit is not in the text. (2) §6.1 gives this inside the frame "Where sources describe regular spraying ... with more in wet weather"; as a separate statement the frame is gone, so read alone it tells any gardener that more spraying is needed in wet weather, which sits against the better-supported view in C-1.

statements.wording: "products" where the sources say "types of fungicides" (UMD-BS) and "active ingredient" (WISC-BS). §6.1 also says "products".
statements.note: Matches §6.1 ("alternating products, to slow resistance"). To know: the AF-12 headline says "alternating or rotating fungicides", and the quotations are about the type or active ingredient, not the product: UMD-BS: "alternate types of fungicides."; WISC-BS: "DO NOT use the same active ingredient for all treatments." Two products can share an active ingredient, so "products" is looser than the sources.

statements.wording: ok against C-2 and §6.1. "so I give both": the views are named but not attributed or described.
statements.rules: Rule 2 (evenly split: both views, lead with neither): met in form. In the answer as ordered, the regular-spraying material (items 2 to 5) comes before this statement.
statements.note: Matches §6.1 on C-2 ("neither view is clearly better supported. Pip gives both and leads with neither"). To know: the statement says "so I give both" but only names the two positions in one clause; it does not say who holds either, and nothing else in this answer sets out the "only when a problem appears" view (ROSS-SP: "should only occur minimally and when the problems are really bad"; SPR: spray "when they are attacked by a particular pest or disease"). Items 2 to 5 of the same answer describe regular spraying and come first, which sits uneasily with "leads with neither". Shown alone, "I give both" promises something the statement does not contain.

statements.rules: Rule 7 wording met. ARC §7 item 5 only partly met: "use only a product labelled for roses where they live" is not in the reminder.
statements.note: ARC §7 item 5 says: "Wherever a spray is described, tell the gardener to use only a product labelled for roses where they live and to follow its label (rule 7)", and §6.2 R-1 says the same. This reminder gives "follow its label and your local rules" but not "use only a product labelled for roses where they live"; that sentence appears only in PKR-CGD-000014 item 2. The reminder itself matches rule 7 ("follow the label and the local rules").

statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated): commercial sources and the 1996 date not stated. Rule 4: no source named in the text.
statements.note: Matches AF-25, including the range of strength ("highly recommended" NZRS-W; "You might also like to" GA-RP). Place is NZ and AU, as required. To know: AF-25 is Moderate and its §4A limitations are not in the text: "Four sources are commercial; the NZ Rose Society article dates from 1996; no institutional source in the UK or US describes it (AF-29)". The last is covered by item 9 and the untested effect by item 8 in the same answer; the commercial sources and the 1996 date are not said anywhere. "Rose sources" is the finding's term, but the eight include a broadcaster (three segments) and a garden-products company. Rule 4 says local information is shown "with the source named"; no source is named in this text.

statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated) and rule 4 (source named): three sources, a broadcaster and two companies, not named or described in the text.
statements.note: Matches AF-26. Place is NZ and AU, as required. To know: AF-26 is Moderate with the §4A limitation "A broadcaster and two companies." (GA-LOOK, TRE-BS, SPR); the text says "Sources say" and names none (rule 4: "with the source named"). "the winter spray" refers back to item 1.

statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated): that three of four sources are commercial, and the 1996 date, are not stated. Rule 4 met: sources named.
statements.decisions: No spray brand, amount or recipe. Company names appear as sources (Tui, South Pacific Roses, Ross Roses); Tui also sells spray products (§8.1).
statements.note: The four sources match AF-36 (NZRS-W, TUI, SPR, ROSS-SP), and "often with a spraying oil" matches the headline (§4A: "two of them name oil with it"). Place is NZ and AU, as required. To know: (1) SPR's copper is applied "At first sign of new spring growth", not in winter after pruning; the finding itself counts it. (2) The text does not say that three of the four are companies (§4A: "Three of the four sources are commercial; the NZ Rose Society article dates from 1996; no source measures the effect"); TUI is "Commercial (garden products)" and §8.1 notes it sells spray products. Naming a company as a source is not naming a spray brand, so the Founder decision on brand names is not broken, but the same answer set also says "I don't name brands" (PKR-CGD-000011 item 6), and Tui is a brand a gardener will see on spray products.

statements.wording: Follows the headline. "use" covers sources that recommend or describe it. Read alone, "with ... the other winter sprays" sits against the AF-41 precaution.
statements.rules: Rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated): "Three of the four sources are commercial" not stated. Rule 4 met: sources named.
statements.decisions: As item 4: company names appear as sources; Tui also sells spray products (§8.1).
statements.note: The four sources match AF-38. Place is NZ and AU, as required. To know: (1) "use" is looser than the quotations for two of them: NZRS-W recommends ("Don't forget a post prune spray of copper and oil"), TUI says they "are effective as clean up sprays". (2) "with or after the other winter sprays" matches the headline, but shown alone it could be read as allowing oil with lime sulphur, which AF-41 says must never be done (item 7 of the same answer). (3) As at item 4: three of the four are companies, not said; Tui is named.

statements.use: ok. First sentence states the gap; second sentence is from AF-14 and is directed by §6.1.
statements.wording: "not a statement that winter sprays don't work" (AF-29) is not carried. "Their winter advice" generalises from UCIPM-DIS (AF-29) by way of AF-14.
statements.note: AF-29 is "Available to Pip only to say there is a gap". The first sentence does that and "I checked" keeps it to the pages opened. The second sentence goes beyond stating the gap, but §6.1 directs it ("Pip says so and gives the winter clear-up") and it rests on AF-14 (Very High, available). To know: (1) "Their winter advice": AF-29 quotes dormant-season sanitation from UCIPM-DIS only; the wider "their" rests on AF-14 (RHS-BS autumn; CLEM-DIS "In the fall or winter"; UMD-BS). (2) §4 adds "This is an absence across the pages opened, not a statement that winter sprays don't work"; the second half of that is not in the text. (3) §6.1 frames this for "Gardeners in the UK and the US"; here place is empty, so everyone sees it, including gardeners whose place is unknown (who see nothing else on winter sprays except the label reminder). §3 puts no place condition on AF-29, so this is allowed. (4) statements.json carries confidence "Low" (correct for AF-29), while the package says the level is not shown for this statement.

statements.wording: Follows the headline. The context "under botrytis blight ... It describes no spray after pruning" (§4, §4A, §8.1) is dropped.
statements.note: Matches the AF-45 headline, place is US only, and it says only one source was found, as §3 requires. To know: the statement sits under "What about a winter spray after pruning?", but §4 says of CLEM-DIS: "under botrytis blight ... It describes no spray after pruning (AF-29)", §4A gives the limitation "Single source; stated under botrytis blight", and §8.1 repeats that it appears "under botrytis blight, not as a spray after pruning". That context is in the package's Limitation column but not in the gardener-facing words, so a US gardener could take it as support for a general winter spray after pruning.

statements.rules: Rule 7 wording met. ARC §7 item 5 only partly met: "use only a product labelled for roses where they live" is not in the reminder.
statements.note: ARC §7 item 5 says: "Wherever a spray is described, tell the gardener to use only a product labelled for roses where they live and to follow its label (rule 7)", and §6.2 R-1 says the same. This reminder gives "follow its label and your local rules" but not "use only a product labelled for roses where they live"; that sentence appears only in PKR-CGD-000014 item 2. The reminder itself matches rule 7 ("follow the label and the local rules").

statements.wording: Follows the headline. No attribution; the limitation "No Australian or US regulator page was read" is dropped.
statements.rules: Rule 7 met. Rule 1 (says that sources say it) and rule §3 (Moderate: limits stated) not met in the text.
statements.note: First sentence matches the AF-34 headline; second sentence is the instruction §6.2 R-1 and §7 item 5 direct ("use only a product labelled for roses where they live"), and it points to the label, so it is not an instruction of Pip's own in place of the label. To know: (1) the first sentence is stated as fact with no "sources say" (rule 1: "never presents it as certain"); (2) "Each country" rests on a UK source (RHS-CHEM) and a New Zealand source (EPA-NZ) only: §4 "No Australian or US regulator page was read", and that §4A limitation of a Moderate finding is not in the text; (3) R-1 (which spray types are approved in each country was not established) is not said here as a gap.

statements.wording: Plural attribution of a claim §4 shows one source making (UCIPM-INS: "with only moderate impact on natural enemies"). CLEM-INS quotation covers soap only.
statements.rules: Rule 1 (how strong the agreement is): one source presented as several. Rule §3: the §4A limit ("Three sources; the nursery is commercial") is not stated.
statements.note: "US university sources say ... with only a moderate effect on aphids' natural enemies": §4 shows one source saying this. UCIPM-INS: "can also be used to suppress aphids with only moderate impact on natural enemies." The other US university source, CLEM-INS, is quoted only as "Insecticidal soap must be sprayed onto the aphids to be effective." (soap only, nothing on natural enemies or oils). The third AF-23 source is a nursery (ROSS-SP). The finding's own claim is "Insecticidal soaps and horticultural oils are described as lower-impact aphid sprays", and §6.1 says "lower-impact sprays"; the builder replaced that with UC IPM's wording and attributed it to "US university sources" in the plural. Supported wording: either attribute "only moderate impact on natural enemies" to the University of California alone, or use the finding's "described as lower-impact aphid sprays" with its three sources (§4A: "Two extension services and one nursery state it").

statements.wording: "kill" where the finding says "harm"; §4 shows one source (CLEM-INS) saying "kill", UCIPM-INS "may harm", UMD-PROB "impacts".
statements.rules: Rule 1 and rule 8: a strength several sources do not agree on.
statements.note: "kill" is stronger than the finding. AF-24 headline: "Broad-spectrum insecticides harm natural enemies and can lead to repeat pest outbreaks"; §6.1: "harm natural enemies and can bring pests back". Only one source says "kill" (CLEM-INS: "these insecticides kill the natural enemies of rose aphids."). The others: UMD-PROB: "minimize impacts on natural enemies, or else secondary (recurring) pest outbreaks can be problematic"; UCIPM-INS: soil-applied systemic insecticides "may harm pollinators and natural enemies." So "Sources say ... kill" puts one source's stronger word on all three. Supported wording: "harm", as the finding and §6.1 have it. A one-word matter; the rest of the statement is supported.

statements.rules: Rule 7 wording met. ARC §7 item 5 only partly met: "use only a product labelled for roses where they live" is not in the reminder.
statements.note: ARC §7 item 5 says: "Wherever a spray is described, tell the gardener to use only a product labelled for roses where they live and to follow its label (rule 7)", and §6.2 R-1 says the same. This reminder gives "follow its label and your local rules" but not "use only a product labelled for roses where they live"; that sentence appears only in PKR-CGD-000014 item 2. The reminder itself matches rule 7 ("follow the label and the local rules").

package.coverage: All 41 findings whose Use status is some form of "Available to Pip" are cited in the trace of at least one statement; none is unused. Partial uses to know: AF-28 is used only for its precaution half (correct for its Use status; the "sources differ on the order and spacing" half is not said); the "lower-toxicity" label of AF-21 and the "lower-impact" label of AF-23 are not used; AF-30 and AF-34 are stated in substance only in PKR-CGD-000014 items 1 and 2 and elsewhere appear as the label reminder.
package.misuse: None found. AF-13, AF-27, AF-35, AF-43 and R-5 appear in no trace and none of their content appears in any text. Nearest points, all acceptable: the pointer to a local rose society in PKR-CGD-000009 item 8 comes from R-3 and rule 5, not AF-35; "clean-up spray" in PKR-CGD-000013 item 1 is AF-25's own term and the purpose claim of AF-27 is not made; PKR-CGD-000012 item 6 names the "only when a problem appears" view without using AF-13.
package.gaps: R-2: said (PKR-CGD-000013 item 8), to NZ and AU only. R-3: said, with a pointer to a local rose society (PKR-CGD-000009 item 8), to NZ only. R-4: said (PKR-CGD-000012 item 7), to NZ only. R-1: said only in part. PKR-CGD-000011 item 3 says it of the synthetic fungicides only and only for "other countries", although R-1 covers all spray types in "New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US". No statement tells a gardener that it was not established whether copper, lime sulphur, oils, sulfur or potassium bicarbonate products are currently approved for home gardeners where they live; PKR-CGD-000014 item 2 gives the practical consequence (approvals change; use only a product labelled for roses where you live) without saying the gap. Rule 5 as written says Pip "says so and points the gardener to local expert help": only the R-3 statement points anywhere; the R-1, R-2, R-4 and AF-29 statements do not. The ARC's "until then" lines for R-1, R-2 and R-4 do not ask for a pointer, so the builder followed the ARC.
package.conflicts: C-1: handled as §6.1 says (PKR-CGD-000009 items 1 to 5 first, item 6 names who disagrees, item 7 gives the RHS). The RHS statement is not marked as part of the disagreement, but the RHS is named. C-2: said as a disagreement with neither view better supported (PKR-CGD-000012 item 6), as §6.1 says; the two views are named but not attributed, and the "only when a problem appears" view is not otherwise set out in that answer. C-3: a gardener would not learn of it. Items 2 and 3 of PKR-CGD-000009 give both findings, but nothing says sources differ on how long resistance lasts or that the Auckland experience contrasts with the RHS. The builder's triage calls this "Better-supported view first (rule 2)"; §6.1 does not state a better-supported view for C-3 and simply lists both findings. C-4: handled (PKR-CGD-000010 items 5 and 6, with the RHS caveat). C-5: handled as §6.1 says. NZ and AU gardeners see both sides (PKR-CGD-000013 items 1 to 9); UK, US and place-unknown gardeners see only that the institutional pages checked describe no spray after pruning, and are not told that NZ and AU sources describe one (rule 4). C-6: a gardener would not learn of it. Only the two precautions (AF-28, AF-41) are shown; that sources differ on the order and timing of the winter sprays is not said anywhere. §6.1 does not ask for more. C-7: handled as a range with the label (PKR-CGD-000012 item 4); the "two- to three-week intervals" of Auckland Botanic Gardens' former programme recorded in C-7 is outside the range shown, as it is in AF-9 and §6.1. C-8: handled as §6.1 says, both views given (PKR-CGD-000011 item 4); the RNZIH view ("really just a safer alternative rather than a panacea") is left out.
other: Results: 29 Pass, 22 Pass with a note, 4 Fail (PKR-CGD-000009 item 4, PKR-CGD-000010 item 1, PKR-CGD-000015 item 2, PKR-CGD-000015 item 3). Two of the Fails (000015 items 2 and 3) are wording the builder changed from §6.1; the other two follow §6.1 and fail on what the §4 quotations and §4A show.

The limitations are not in the gardener-facing words. The package has a "Limitation" column per statement, but statements.json (the exact words shown) does not carry it. Rule §3 allows a Moderate finding "with its limits stated". Unless the app shows that column, the §4A limits of these Moderate findings are not stated to the gardener: AF-3 (000009 item 3), AF-8 (000010 item 1), AF-11 (000012 item 3), AF-20 (000010 item 8), AF-23 (000015 item 2), AF-25 (000013 item 1), AF-26 (000013 item 2), AF-34 (000014 item 2), AF-36 and AF-38 (000013 items 4 and 5, commercial sources), and the source-type limit of AF-16 (000010 item 4). For AF-45 (000013 item 10) the "under botrytis blight" context is likewise only in that column.

Statements that mislead or lose meaning when shown alone: 000009 item 6 ("The view above is the better supported"); 000010 item 6 ("Powdery mildew is the exception"); 000012 item 6 ("so I give both"); 000012 item 3 (loses the "where sources describe regular spraying" frame that §6.1 gives it); 000013 items 2, 3 and 4 ("the winter spray" refers to item 1); 000013 item 5 ("with or after the other winter sprays" without the AF-41 precaution); 000013 item 9 ("Their winter advice"); 000013 item 10 (without item 9, reads as support for a winter spray).

The label reminder repeated in 000011 item 8, 000012 item 8, 000013 item 11 and 000015 item 4 says "follow its label and your local rules" but not "use only a product labelled for roses where they live", which ARC §7 item 5 asks for "Wherever a spray is described". That sentence is only in 000014 item 2. PKR-CGD-000009 (which mentions fungicides and regular spraying) carries no label reminder at all.

Rule 4 says local information is shown "with the source named". 000013 items 1 and 2 (NZ and AU only) name no source in their text, and 000013 item 7 says "One New Zealand rose nursery" without naming it. This is met only if the app shows the record's supporting sources alongside.

Company names as sources: 000013 items 4 and 5 name Tui, South Pacific Roses and Ross Roses. These are sources, not spray brands, so Founder decision 1 (no brand names) is not broken, but Tui is a garden-products company that sells sprays (§8.1), and 000011 item 6 tells the gardener "I don't name brands". The text does not say these three are companies.

Precautions shown to everyone: 000014 items 6 and 7 (lime sulphur with copper; lime sulphur with oil) have no place limit, which their Use status allows. Gardeners outside NZ and AU are not shown the winter-spray findings these precautions belong to (AF-36, AF-37, AF-38). The AF-28 precaution rests on NZRS-W, which §8.1 records as "a 1996 article; product availability may have changed since"; that is not said.
